posts.title: A five-year wallet came home
posts.excerpt: A bifold we sewed in 2021 came back this week for one opened seam. The leather had done the rest of the work.
posts.content:
A bifold we sewed in 2021 came back this week for one opened seam. The leather had done the rest of the work.

Five years in a back pocket

It left the bench the colour of pale biscuit. It came back deep chestnut, soft as a glove, with a gloss on the fold no polish could give.

One seam at the note sleeve had opened where a key had rubbed through the thread. Everything else held.

Twenty minutes of work

We picked out the old thread, kept the original holes and restitched with the same waxed linen. Covered for life, so no charge.

The stitches are ours; the colour is all his.

Teo Ishida

posts.title: Indigo dye day
posts.excerpt: Twice a year we dye a batch of hides in our own indigo vat. Eight dips, two days, blue hands for a week.
posts.content:
Twice a year we dye a batch of hides in our own indigo vat. Eight dips, two days, blue hands for a week.

Why eight dips

Indigo builds in layers. One dip gives a pale sky; eight give the ink blue of our long wallet. Between dips the hide hangs to oxidise from green to blue.

The second hide always comes out darker: the vat is warmest on the second morning.

How it ages

Indigo does not darken like natural leather. It softens at the folds into the blue of old denim.

posts.title: Six new hides from upriver
posts.excerpt: The autumn shoulders arrived from the tannery: six hides, tanned for six weeks in chestnut and mimosa bark.
posts.content:
The autumn shoulders arrived from the tannery: six hides, tanned for six weeks in chestnut and mimosa bark.

Choosing a hide

We look for tight grain at the shoulder, few scars and an even thickness. Small marks from the animal’s life stay; they are part of the leather.

Each hide gives about twelve wallets, or two totes and the straps for them.

Resting

New hides rest flat in the back room for two weeks before the first cut, so they settle to the room.

posts.title: Restitching a tote handle
posts.excerpt: A market tote from another maker came in with a handle hanging by one rivet. We replaced it from the same kind of hide.
posts.content:
A market tote from another maker came in with a handle hanging by one rivet. We replaced it from the same kind of hide.

Matching old leather

A new handle on an old bag looks pale at first. We chose a piece of natural shoulder and left it in the sun for a week before stitching.

In a year nobody will know which handle is new.

The cost

A new handle with stitching and rivets: $55, three weeks at the bench.

posts.title: Two needles, one thread
posts.excerpt: Why we still sew every seam by hand with a saddle stitch, and what it has to do with a cut thread.
posts.content:
Why we still sew every seam by hand with a saddle stitch, and what it has to do with a cut thread.

The stitch

A machine stitch is one thread looped under another; cut it and the seam unzips. A saddle stitch runs two needles through each hole from both sides.

If one thread is cut, the other still holds the seam closed until it can be mended.

The thread

Waxed linen, twisted in three strands. It softens with the leather and darkens with it.

posts.title: Riverside Lane in autumn
posts.excerpt: The lane outside the workshop smells of wet stone and bark this month. A short note on leather and the change of season.
posts.content:
The lane outside the workshop smells of wet stone and bark this month. A short note on leather and the change of season.

Damp weeks

Leather drinks the air. In the wet weeks before winter, let a rained-on bag dry slowly, away from the stove, then give it a little balm.

Open days

From November the workshop opens at noon on Thursdays. Saturdays stay the same.
